papers.title: Sleepless nights: Caregiver burden among DLB patients with nighttime behaviors in the PACE-DLB Cohort
papers.abstract: Background Nighttime behaviors in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) may increase caregiver burden by disrupting sleep and respite. Objective To examine associations between nighttime-behavior severity, caregiver burden, caregiving time, and caregiver well-being in moderate-to-advanced DLB. Methods We analyzed baseline data from 188 patient-caregiver dyads in the multicenter PACE-DLB cohort. Nighttime behaviors were categorized as mild/absent or moderate/severe using the Neuropsychiatric Inventory Questionnaire. Caregiver burden was assessed using the shortened Zarit Burden Interview (sZBI). Secondary outcomes included caregiving time and well-being. Group comparisons and exploratory multivariable regression were performed. Results Moderate-to-severe nighttime behaviors were reported in 117 individuals (62.2%). Caregivers in this group reported more hours on duty daily (median 24 [IQR 15-24] vs 13 [6-24]; p=0.004), more time in the same room (6 vs 3 hours/day; p=0.011), and greater burden (median sZBI 21 [13-26] vs 18 [12-21]; p=0.015). Exploratory comparisons identified differences in prioritizing care recipients' needs (p=0.046) and caregiver sleep disruption (p=0.010). After adjustment for other neuropsychiatric symptoms and patient characteristics, the nighttime-behavior association was attenuated (beta=1.5, 95% CI -0.93 to 3.9; p=0.20), whereas anxiety remained associated with greater burden (beta=3.5, 95% CI 1.2-5.9; p=0.004). Conclusions Nighttime behaviors were associated with greater caregiver burden and caregiving demands in unadjusted analyses. Although the adjusted burden association was attenuated, nighttime behaviors may impose distinct challenges through increased supervision and disrupted caregiver sleep. Further studies are needed to determine whether interventions targeting nighttime behaviors can reduce caregiving burden.

papers.title: Predicting pediatric stroke outcomes using adult lesion-symptom models
papers.abstract: Lesion location is a key predictor of post-stroke outcomes in adults, but its relevance for predicting childhood stroke outcomes is unclear. Recent developmental neuroscience work suggests that the gross spatial organization of large-scale brain systems may be generally conserved across development, raising the possibility that damage to common anatomical substrates might underlie chronic domain-level impairments after both adult-onset and childhood stroke. If so, then it should be possible to leverage adult lesion-symptom relationships to predict chronic childhood stroke outcomes. We tested the hypothesis that lesion-symptom models trained to predict sensorimotor and language impairments in patients with adult-onset brain lesions can be translated to predict chronic sensorimotor and language outcomes after childhood stroke. We trained multivariate lesion-symptom models to predict sensorimotor (Grooved Peg-Board Test: N=463; median age=53.6, IQR=17.9 years) and language (Token Test: N=379; median age=53.2, IQR=19.4 years) impairments in patients with adult-onset brain lesions. We applied the trained models to lesion segmentations from childhood stroke survivors enrolled in the SCOUTS Study (N=469; median age=9.3, IQR=11.0 years), resulting in outcome predictions that we compared against chronic (6+ month) measures of sensorimotor and language impairment derived from the Pediatric Stroke Outcome Measure and the Recurrence and Recovery Questionnaire. The adult lesion-symptom models generated outcome predictions that robustly correlated with pediatric impairment scores (sensorimotor: rho=0.43; language: rho=0.42; PFWE <0.001), enabled classification of pediatric impairment status (both AUC=0.76; PFWE=0.004), and afforded unique predictive power in multivariable pediatric outcome models (sensorimotor: adjusted OR=3.6, 95% CI=2.4-5.2; language: adjusted OR=3.0, 95% CI=1.67-5.30). Lesion-symptom models trained using pediatric lesion and outcome data captured robust lesion-symptom relationships (both rhocv=0.40, P<0.001), but yielded no advantage over the adult model predictions when compared directly via cross-validation in the pediatric cohort. Further, the adult and pediatric models made similar predictions when applied to the same lesion data even after adjusting for common effects of lesion size and laterality, suggesting a general convergence towards common anatomical signals present in both children and adults. Lesion-symptom models trained in patients with adult-onset brain lesions can be translated across outcome measures and developmental stages to predict chronic sensorimotor and language impairments after childhood stroke. These results establish lesion location as an important predictor of childhood stroke outcomes, demonstrate the feasibility of translating adult lesion-symptom models for chronic outcome prediction in children, and support the broader conclusion that the critical anatomy underlying post-stroke sensorimotor and language impairments may be generally conserved across development.

papers.title: Effects of age and lesion characteristics on chronic outcomes after childhood stroke: a large-scale study of 469 childhood stroke survivors
papers.abstract: The effects of stroke on the developing brain are thought to depend on age at stroke onset, but the nature of this relationship is unclear. While it has been suggested that younger age at stroke onset might facilitate recovery, there is also evidence that critical developmental periods in early childhood confer increased vulnerability to injury. Associations between age at stroke onset and childhood stroke outcomes are mixed and often inconsistent, and the roles of lesion factors such as size, laterality and location are poorly understood. We investigated how age and lesion factors relate to chronic (6+ months post-onset) sensorimotor, expressive language, receptive language, and cognitive/behavioral impairments in 469 childhood stroke survivors enrolled in the SCOUTS study (median age at stroke=9.3 years; 57% male). We used ordinal logistic regression models to characterize associations between outcomes and age at stroke onset, left and right hemispheric lesion volumes, and years to chronic assessment, and we used voxel-based lesion-symptom correlations to evaluate associations with lesion location. We also tested whether age at stroke onset moderates relationships between lesion factors and chronic outcomes. When considered in isolation, younger age at stroke onset was significantly associated with worse outcomes across all domains, but in multivariable models, statistically significant associations were observed only for language outcomes. Larger lesion volumes in each hemisphere were significantly associated with worse contralateral sensorimotor outcomes and with worse language and cognitive/behavioral outcomes. For language outcomes, associations with lesion volume were strongest for the left hemisphere, and older age at stroke onset amplified the detrimental effect of large left hemisphere lesions on expressive language outcomes. Lesion-symptom analyses mapped sensorimotor impairments to structures including the putamen, sensorimotor cortices, superior parietal cortex, and cortico-spinal projections. Expressive and receptive language impairments both mapped to mostly left-lateralized and partially overlapping frontal, temporal and parietal structures, with the strongest associations in the white matter underlying left posterior temporo-parietal areas. Cognitive/behavioral impairments mapped to bilateral regions associated with action mode and somato-cognitive action networks including right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, left inferior frontal and supramarginal gyri, and inter-effector nodes of the right pre-central gyrus. These results provide novel insights into how age at stroke onset and lesion factors contribute to childhood stroke outcomes, map domain-level impairments to specific lesion locations, and indicate that the vulnerability of left hemisphere language networks to injury may increase as language becomes more left-lateralized during development.

papers.title: Neurometabolite Changes Following Football Heading: A 7 T Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy Study
papers.abstract: Background/Hypothesis Concern is growing around the effects of repeated non-concussive head impacts from football heading, but it is unclear whether a single bout of heading alters neurochemistry. Neurometabolite levels were measured with 7 T proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy with the primary motor cortex before and after controlled heading. Methods In a within-subject, repeated measures study, 20 participants (15 male; mean [SD] age of 25.2 [6.6]), with no reported history of head injury in the past year or any neurological conditions, performed 20 controlled rotational headers. Proton spectra were acquired at three timepoints: one before heading (Pre) and twice after heading (Post_1 and Post_2). Neurometabolite absolute molal concentrations (mol/Kg) were used as the main outcome. Results N-acetylaspartate (NAA) showed a significant effect of Time [F(2, 36.7) = 8.01, pFDR < 0.01] with elevated levels at the Post_2 timepoints compared with both Pre and Post_1 measurements. No other metabolites showed significant changes. Conclusion An acute bout of 20 headers was associated with detectable changes in NAA concentration levels. This finding from 7 T MRS provides valuable insight into the neurochemical changes resultant from repeated non-concussive head impacts, which may be suggestive of an acute neuronal response to heading. This study was registered with the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS00029600)

papers.title: Putative Causal Effects of Amyloid-β on GFAP: a Mendelian Randomization Study
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) is a marker of astrocytic activation that correlates with cerebral Alzheimer disease (AD) pathology. The causal relationship between GFAP elevation and amyloid-{beta} remains unclear. We examined whether A{beta} drives GFAP elevation and whether GFAP is independently associated with AD progression. METHODS: In the Harvard Aging Brain Study (HABS; n=329 cognitively unimpaired participants) and the Religious Orders Study and Rush Memory and Aging Project (ROSMAP; n=835 deceased participants spanning cognitively unimpaired to dementia), we performed one-sample Mendelian randomization. APOE {epsilon}4 served as the instrumental variable to estimate the causal effect of A{beta} (PET in HABS; immunohistochemistry in ROSMAP) on GFAP (plasma in HABS; brain mRNA expression in ROSMAP). Linear regression and linear mixed-effects models assessed GFAP associations with tau, hippocampal atrophy, and cognitive decline. RESULTS: In both cohorts, Mendelian randomization supported a causal effect of A{beta} on GFAP (HABS {beta} = 0.37; 95% CI, 0.11 to 0.63; P=6.1x10-3; ROSMAP {beta} = 0.35; 95% CI, 0.12 to 0.59; P=3.3x10-3). In HABS, GFAP associations with tau and cognition were no longer significant after adjusting for A{beta}, and GFAP was not associated with hippocampal atrophy. In ROSMAP, GFAP remained associated with tau and cognition after A{beta} adjustment, but not with cognition after additional adjustment for tau. DISCUSSION: Brain GFAP gene expression and plasma GFAP elevation may be downstream consequences of A{beta} accumulation. GFAP showed little independent association with cognition once core AD pathology was accounted for. These findings refine the interpretation of elevated plasma GFAP in AD.

papers.title: Altered Auditory Network Differentiation in Multiple Sclerosis: A BROAD-NESS MEG Study
papers.abstract: The auditory P300 is widely used at the sensor level to study cognitive dysfunction in multiple sclerosis (MS), but its brain generators have rarely been investigated. The three-stimulus oddball separates task relevance from stimulus rarity, and source-level network analysis can show where and when this distinction is altered. We recorded magnetoencephalography (MEG) in 20 MS patients and 15 healthy controls during a three-stimulus auditory oddball with standard, target and non-target tones. Broadband networks were estimated from beamformer source activity with BROAD-NESS, a principal component analysis of group-averaged sources. Groups were compared with cluster-based permutation tests corrected across networks. Four networks explained 94% of the variance. Sensory (N1m) and P3 responses and task performance did not differ between groups. In a bilateral perisylvian and sensorimotor network, the difference between target and non-target responses was smaller in patients than in controls at about 370 to 500 ms (cluster p = 0.020, corrected across networks; Hedges' g = -1.11 and Bayes factor 16.1 in the localizer window). A conventional source-by-source analysis of the same contrast found no cluster surviving correction. The effect was robust to leave-one-out analysis, an alternative network estimation and excluding participants with clinical or recording characteristics, but did not survive correction across all three contrasts (p = 0.108). Network measures were not related to discrimination performance or fatigue, and no exploratory correlation with clinical or cognitive measures survived correction. In MS, task-related source-level networks were largely preserved, but one network differentiated less between task-relevant and task-irrelevant deviants, without a behavioural deficit.

papers.title: Decreased thermal contrast sensitivity for paradoxical heat sensation in diabetic polyneuropathy
papers.abstract: Paradoxical heat sensation (PHS), the perception of warmth during cooling, is typically induced by alternating warm and cold stimulation. Recent work has demonstrated that thermal contrast, defined as the difference between alternating temperatures, is a key determinant of this phenomenon in healthy individuals. However, it remains unclear whether peripheral sensory loss changes the thermal contrast required to elicit PHS and whether the experience itself remains the same after such sensory loss. We investigated PHS in individuals with probable diabetic polyneuropathy (DPN; N = 32) and healthy controls (N = 42) using a pre-registered Bayesian computational model. The model related the probability of a warm report to thermal contrast and used response times and confidence ratings as markers of perceptual uncertainty. Although prevalence was similar between groups, the thermal contrast required to elicit PHS was higher in patients with DPN, reaching the midpoint of the psychometric function at approximately 51% thermal contrast in healthy controls and 80% in patients with DPN. In both groups, warm reports were accompanied by greater uncertainty, reflected in longer response times and lower confidence. This pattern suggests that PHS does not typically reflect a clear sensation of warmth but rather an ambiguous thermal experience. These findings show that the sensation is accompanied by perceptual uncertainty in both groups, while patients with DPN require greater thermal contrast to elicit it.

papers.title: An updated open-source, large dataset of T1-weighted stroke brain MRIs and lesion segmentation masks
papers.abstract: Precise delineation of stroke lesions on MRI scans provides essential quantitative information used routinely in stroke rehabilitation research. Manual annotation continues to be the gold standard for stroke lesion delineation but is subjective and labor-intensive. Our previous release of ATLAS v2.1 (N=1271) provided a large, open-source dataset of T1w stroke brain MRIs and manually segmented lesion masks, which facilitated the development of numerous lesion segmentation algorithms. However, fully automated algorithm performance is not yet adequate to replace manual protocols; existing lesion segmentation algorithms still lack accuracy and generalizability. As model architectures grow increasingly sophisticated, they demand large-scale, diverse training data. Here, we present ATLAS v3.0 (N=1815), an updated, larger dataset of T1w stroke brain MRIs with corresponding manually segmented lesion masks. ATLAS v3.0 comes with nearly 43% more data, consisting of a publicly accessible, heterogenous training (n=1453), and a hidden generalizability dataset with subjects that remain unreleased (n=362). We anticipate this updated ATLAS v3.0 release will support the growing data demands of advanced lesion segmentation algorithms.

papers.title: Causal Emergence of Macroscopic Stochastic Dynamics from a Multi-modal Foundation Model of Human Sleep
papers.abstract: Sleep is an essential, self organizing physiological state conserved across species, yet its macroscopic coordination remains governed by unknown physical principles. For nearly sixty years, clinical medicine has classified sleep into heuristic, discrete 30 second epochs, an empirical convention that flattens continuous non-equilibrium dynamics and leaves deep subcortical neuromodulatory control fundamentally unobservable. Although emerging artificial intelligence foundation models can decode multimodal physiology with high accuracy, their high-dimensional representations remain uninterpretable black boxes, leaving the generative laws of sleep unformulated. Here we show that, across four independent multinational cohorts, causal emergence analysis of a multimodal foundation model condenses human sleep into a single continuous order parameter whose dynamics are well described by a Landau Ginzburg jump diffusion equation. This trajectory is physiologically structured: its overnight variance follows an AASM stage hierarchy (Wake, NREM, REM), and its diffusion shape tracks apnea hypopnea severity. Bidirectional clinical perturbations further support the decomposition: continuous positive airway pressure lowers baseline diffusion and apnea band spectral excess while shallowing the late-night potential well, whereas GABAergic agonism reduces the true jump rate and nocturnal awakenings without deepening the well. Length matched comparisons under dexmedetomidine sedation deepen the well and suppress jumps relative to natural sleep. By replacing empirical classification with an explicit stochastic description, our work uses a foundation model as a probe of physiological dynamics rather than only as a predictor and treats human sleep as an analytically tractable physical system. More broadly, the finding that multi-organ coordination during sleep can be summarized by a low dimensional order parameter suggests a general route from opaque artificial intelligence representations to testable macroscopic models of the subcortical dynamics that sustain human consciousness and fail in neuropsychiatric disease.

papers.title: Incidence and outcome of intracerebral hemorrhage in a prospective cohort and healthcare data.
papers.abstract: Background: The global burden of intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) remains high. Identifying trends in incidence and outcome requires resource-intensive epidemiological surveillance. Our objective was to characterise incidence, survival and functional outcome of people with ICH in a cohort study; and compare to healthcare systems data (HSD) in the same region. Methods: We conducted a prospective population-based inception cohort study in Lothian, Scotland, UK (the Lothian Audit of Treatment of ICH, LATCH). LATCH included all spontaneous non-traumatic ICH in Lothian residents [≥]16 years between 1st June 2010 - 31st May 2013 and 1st November 2018 - 31st October 2021. We identified and characterized people with ICH in HSD in the same region and period using linked primary and secondary care records, community prescriptions and death records. We calculated incidence per 100,000 person-years; 30-day survival; and sensitivity and positive predictive value of ICH detection in HSD. For functional outcome one year after ICH, we compared the modified Rankin Scale score (mRS) in LATCH to days alive and out of hospital in HSD. Results: In LATCH, from 1283 possible cases, 1021 were first-ever ICH. We identified 876 people with ICH in HSD in the same period. In LATCH, ICH incidence was 23.7 (95%CI 22.2-25.2) per 100,000 person-years (48.5% male, mean age 72 (SD 14.6) years), with no time trend (trend in crude incidence rates 0.31/year (-3.78-4.39)). ICH incidence in HSD was 23.1 (21.6-24.6) per 100,000 person-years (48.3% male, mean age 74.2 (SD 14.0) years). The positive predictive value of ICH identified in HSD versus LATCH was 78.3% (75.4%-81.0%). 30-day case fatality was 41.2% (38.1%-44.2%) in LATCH and 39.0% (35.5%-42.3%) in HSD. We found good correlation between functional outcome measures (Spearman's r=0.88, p<0.001). Conclusions: The burden of ICH remains persistently high. HSD appears accurate for assessing incidence, survival and functional outcome.

papers.title: Cerebrospinal fluid cellular dynamics following modified interval dosing natalizumab therapy in multiple sclerosis
papers.abstract: Background Natalizumab, an 4-integrin monoclonal antibody, a highly effective relapsing multiple sclerosis (MS) therapy, carries a small but clinically important risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). Previous studies have suggested that alternative dosing paradigms can reduce PML risk while maintaining therapeutic efficacy. Objectives Clarify how immune cell dynamics changes with the alternative dosing. Methods We investigated alternative dosing paradigms by profiling cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) immune cell dynamics across: (1) standard interval dosing (SID, every 4 weeks), (2) extended interval dosing (EID, every 6 or 8 weeks), and (3) annual 12-week gap (aGAP). Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we analyzed 46 CSF samples from participants across dosing regimens, untreated MS controls, and one non-natalizumab-related PML case. Results Compared with controls, natalizumab reduced proportions of Treg, memory T cells, B cells, and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, while increasing tissue-resident memory T and microglia-like myeloid cells. EID and aGAP were associated with higher proportions of peripheral immune populations, including CD4+ T cells with interferon response signatures (CD4+IFN+), potentially enhancing antiviral immunity. The PML case exhibited elevated CD8+ central memory T and CD56bright NK cells proportions in the CSF, suggesting their role in viral control. Conclusions These findings support that EID and aGAP allow immune reconstitution.

papers.title: Multicentre electrophysiology reveals the limits of auditory prediction responses as biomarkers of chronic tinnitus
papers.abstract: Identifying reliable neural biomarkers of chronic tinnitus remains challenging because ageing and hearing loss independently influence auditory cortical activity. Here, we investigated auditory expectation processing in 440 adults with (n = 226) and without (n = 214) chronic tinnitus using electroencephalography during a local-global auditory paradigm across six centres. Although several electrophysiological group differences emerged in unadjusted analyses, most were substantially attenuated after adjustment for demographic and audiological factors. Two clusters remained significant within the unexpected-omission-versus-sound contrast (44 to 100 ms and 356 to 476 ms), but neither survived correction across eight contrasts. Direct comparisons between expected and unexpected omissions revealed no significant group differences. Exploratory classification using selected EEG features achieved a cross-validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.624, increasing to 0.689 when combined with demographic and audiological predictors. However, this improvement was not reproduced in held-out validation, and EEG features showed limited predictive value for tinnitus burden or loudness. These findings highlight a fundamental distinction between electrophysiological group differences and clinically informative individual-level biomarkers, underscoring the importance of controlling for confounding factors and establishing independent predictive validity in tinnitus research.

papers.title: Distinct Associations of Gait Variability and Physical Fitness with Resting-State Dynamic Functional Connectivity in Cognitively Normal Older Adults from the AGUEDA Trial
papers.abstract: Gait variability and physical fitness may provide accessible indicators of brain health in aging, yet their associations with resting-state dynamic functional connectivity remain unclear. We examined associations of gait variability and physical fitness with local and distant temporal consistency of resting-state dynamic functional connectivity in 86 cognitively normal older adults from the AGUEDA trial. Gait variability was assessed using coefficients of variation for stride length, gait velocity, step time, and step length, while physical fitness included muscular strength and cardiorespiratory fitness. Dynamic functional connectivity was estimated using voxel-wise stepwise connectivity analyses. Analyses targeting regions related to Alzheimers disease risk and exploratory whole-brain analyses were adjusted for age, sex, and education. Greater gait variability was associated with local, but not distant, temporal consistency of dynamic functional connectivity. Greater stride length, gait velocity, and step length variability were associated with higher local temporal consistency in the left inferior frontal gyrus ({beta} = 0.28 to 0.33; false discovery rate-corrected P = 0.024 to 0.047) and lower temporal consistency in the right insula ({beta} = -0.47 to -0.31; false discovery rate-corrected P = 0.001 to 0.028). Whole-brain analyses revealed lower local temporal consistency in the left parahippocampal gyrus with greater stride length variability ({beta} = -0.43; family-wise error-corrected P = 0.002) and in the left calcarine cortex with greater gait velocity variability ({beta} = -0.45; family-wise error-corrected P = 0.001). No statistically significant associations were observed for physical fitness. These findings suggest that gait variability may reflect aspects of local dynamic functional brain organization in cognitively normal older adults.

papers.title: Continuous at-home wearables and machine learning sensitively track function and progression in pediatric and adult Friedreich's ataxia
papers.abstract: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA) is the most common hereditary ataxia, characterized by progressive cerebellar and sensory ataxia, proprioceptive loss, and upper motor neuron involvement, with onset typically in childhood. Current outcome measures used in clinical trials are limited by rater subjectivity, coarse scoring, infrequent in-person assessments, and inability to assess behavior continuously in naturalistic settings. We tested whether submovement-based measures derived from accelerometers worn continuously at home could sensitively capture motor impairment and disease progression in FRDA across a range of ages and disease severity. 95 participants (57 FRDA, 38 controls; age 2-75) wore GENEActiv wrist and ankle sensors for one week per timepoint; 60 completed two or more timepoints spanning up to 2.2 years. 85 movement features were extracted including submovement kinematics and activity intensity. The FRDA cohort included ambulatory and non-ambulatory participants spanning early, mid, and late stages of disease. Five machine-learned composite models were evaluated, including FRDA-specific models, and models previously trained on other populations. Sensor measures were evaluated for relationships with clinician-rated and patient-reported measures, reliability, and sensitivity to progression. Ankle sensor measures demonstrated strong cross-sectional correlations with Friedreich's Ataxia-Functional Disability Staging (|r| = 0.66-0.87), Modified Friedreich's Ataxia Rating Scale total (|r| = 0.53-0.73), Friedreich's Ataxia-Activities of Daily Living (|r| = 0.58-0.74), and Friedreich's Ataxia-Health Index total (|r| = 0.43-0.57), with high within-week reliability (ICC = 0.89-0.96) and large differences between FRDA and control groups (|e.s.| = 2.0-2.6). FRDA-specific composite outcomes showed significant longitudinal sensitivity to disease progression (|MSDR| = 0.67-0.89), whereas patient global impression of change did not capture progression. At-home ankle accelerometer data yield reliable, ecologically valid measures reflecting clinician-rated and patient-reported outcomes, and capture disease progression in FRDA. These results support remote wearables as sensitive digital outcome measures for FRDA clinical trials and disease monitoring.

papers.title: Automatic cerebral angiographic perfusion analysis
papers.abstract: Purpose: To automate anatomical localization for angiographic perfusion and evaluate agreement with manual processing between biplane projections in a held-out external cohort. Methods: Separate anteroposterior (AP) and lateral projection hemisphere and internal carotid artery (ICA) models used DeepLabv3+ with ResNet50 encoders. Development used patient-separated training, validation, and testing. External patients were excluded from fitting and model selection. Automated pipeline and manual-pipeline perfusion shared downstream calculations. Eligible acquisitions contained at least 7 seconds of data after bolus arrival. Segmentation metrics and Bland-Altman analyses evaluated mean transit time (MTT) and time to maximum of the residue function (Tmax). Results: External segmentation testing included 353 runs from 73 patients. Patient-mean hemisphere Dice was 0.959 (95% CI, 0.952-0.965) in AP and 0.965 (0.960-0.969) in lateral views while ICA Dice was 0.635 (0.617-0.650) and 0.558 (0.534-0.579). Manually processed perfusion comparisons included 165 external runs from 52 patients. Mean absolute differences (95% CI) were 0.39 (0.31-0.47) and 0.32 (0.25-0.40) seconds for AP and lateral MTT, and 0.23 (0.15-0.35) and 0.31 (0.17-0.51) seconds for Tmax. Among 220 external cohort biplane pairs from 61 patients, mean absolute differences were 0.48 seconds (95% CI, 0.42-0.53) for MTT and 0.53 seconds (0.35-0.75) for Tmax. Repeated-measures mean biases (95% CI) were -0.07 (-0.19 to 0.05) and 0.16 seconds (-0.08 to 0.40), with 95% limits of agreement of -1.38 to 1.24 and -2.65 to 2.97 seconds respectively. Conclusion: Our automated perfusion pipeline showed favorable agreement with manually processed results in the external validation cohort. Independently processed biplane views had small average bias.

papers.title: Ecological characterisation of frequency-domain local field potential biomarkers in essential tremor.
papers.abstract: Adaptive deep brain stimulation could make the treatment of essential tremor more responsive to patients' needs, delivering stimulation when tremor-provoking movements occur rather than continuously, thereby potentially reducing habituation-related loss of efficacy and stimulation-induced adverse effects. Its success, however, depends on neural control signals that remain measurable and meaningful long after surgery, at home rather than in the laboratory, and while stimulation is running. Thalamic local field potentials offer such candidate signals, yet they have largely been characterised intraoperatively or in the early postoperative period, under supervised conditions that reveal little about their behaviour in daily life. We therefore followed nine patients with essential tremor implanted with a sensing-enabled neurostimulator targeting the ventral intermediate nucleus and posterior subthalamic area, combining in-clinic recordings three and six months after surgery with weekly, patient-performed home recordings. We extracted 13 spectral features encompassing canonical and tremor-frequency band power, aperiodic spectral properties and periodic beta activity, and evaluated their agreement between home and clinic recordings, between-session reliability and movement-related modulation across recording settings and stimulation states. Oscillatory features did not differ systematically between home and clinic, whereas the aperiodic background was consistently steeper at home and poorly reproducible. Periodic beta measures emerged as the most robust candidates: with stimulation off, their clinic-home reliability approached that observed between the two clinic visits, and a postural task suppressed beta activity across recording settings, an effect carried by the periodic component rather than by the aperiodic background. Stimulation, however, reduced the reliability of beta measures and markedly attenuated their movement-related modulation, precisely under the conditions in which an adaptive controller would need to operate. Within the limits of this small cohort, thalamic beta activity therefore appears unlikely to serve as a stand-alone control signal for adaptive stimulation in essential tremor, highlighting the potential need for complementary cortical or peripheral inputs.

papers.title: Parkinson's disease-associated LRRK2 armadillo domain variants enhance kinase pathway activity through a Rab-binding site-dependent mechanism
papers.abstract: Pathogenic variants that increase LRRK2 kinase activity are a common genetic cause of Parkinson's disease. Most pathogenic variants occur within the catalytic ROC-COR GTPase (e.g. R1441C) and kinase (e.g. G2019S) domains, where they activate LRRK2 through distinct mechanisms. The common kinase-domain variant directly enhances the intrinsic catalytic activity of LRRK2, whereas ROC-COR variants shift the equilibrium towards its active conformation. Whether variants in the N-terminal armadillo (ARM) domain, which contains Rab GTPase-binding sites involved in LRRK2 membrane recruitment, activate LRRK2 through a different mechanism remains unclear. Here, we characterise the LRRK2 Madrid haplotype, comprising two ARM variants (L119P/L488P) identified in a multigenerational family with PD. In cellular assays, L488P, but not L119P, increased LRRK2-mediated Rab10 phosphorylation approximately two-fold. Increased LRRK2 pathway activity was likewise observed in primary neutrophils and monocytes from variant carriers, including individuals with and without PD. Multiplexed parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) mass spectrometry in neutrophils further demonstrated coordinated increases in phosphorylation of six endogenous Rab substrates (Rab3, Rab8, Rab10, Rab12, Rab35 and Rab43), demonstrating concordant pathway activation in cellular models and primary human blood cells. Mechanistically, L488P lies adjacent to ARM Rab-binding site 1, and its activating effect was abolished by the site-1-disrupting L403E substitution, whereas activation by the ROC-domain variant R1441C was retained. We further investigated five rare ARM-domain variants identified through GP2 and independent genetic datasets, of which two, F470S and V483G, showed increased LRRK2 pathway activity in a site-1-dependent manner, while the remaining three showed no substantial activation. Together, these findings demonstrate that L488P-mediated pathway activation is recapitulated in human variant carriers and depends on an intact ARM Rab-binding site 1, identifying a mechanism of LRRK2 regulation distinct from that of classical catalytic-core variants.

papers.title: Dynamic Macro-Microvascular Coupling During Cerebrovascular Reactivity Revealed by Simultaneous TCD and DCS
papers.abstract: Background Transcranial Doppler (TCD) measures flow velocity in large intracranial arteries but provides limited information on microvascular perfusion.Diffuse correlation spectroscopy (DCS) enables continuous, noninvasive assessment of cortical microvascular blood flow. We compared macrovascular and microvascular responses during cerebrovascular reactivity testing. Methods Forty-four healthy adults (28 men; mean age, 27.0{+/-}3.8 years) underwent simultaneous bilateral TCD and DCS during a breath-holding task (1-minute baseline, 30-second breath hold, and 1-minute recovery). Middle cerebral artery flow velocity and cortical microvascular blood flow index were normalized to baseline (rCBFv and rCBFi, respectively). Temporal responses were compared using Pearson correlation and Bland-Altman analyses. Response amplitude, rise time, and recovery time were also assessed. Results TCD and DCS showed concordant response trajectories during breath holding and recovery. Correlations between normalized temporal responses were strong in both hemispheres (left,r=0.988{+/-}0.009;right, r=0.990{+/-}0.008; both P<0.001). Bland-Altman analysis showed minimal systematic bias and no proportional bias. No significant interhemispheric differences were observed in response amplitude, rise time, or recovery time. DCS-derived rCBFi showed greater response amplitudes and variability than TCD-derived rCBFv (left, 1.80{+/-}0.34 vs 1.63{+/-}0.15; right, 1.72{+/-}0.27 vs 1.63{+/-}0.14). Parameter-level analyses showed strong correlations and minimal bias for response amplitude, rise time, and recovery time. Conclusions TCD and DCS demonstrated strong temporal coupling during cerebrovascular reactivity testing, while DCS detected larger response amplitudes than TCD. These findings suggest that macrovascular velocity and cortical microvascular perfusion provide complementary information about cerebrovascular responses.

papers.title: Nigral volume as a marker for Lewy body copathology in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: BackgroundLewy body (LB) copathology in Alzheimers disease (AD) is associated with earlier symptom onset and faster cognitive decline. Depigmentation of substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) volume is seen in both Parkinsons disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. We examined whether lower antemortem SNc volume was associated with autopsy confirmed LB pathology in patients with AD or mild cognitive impairment (MCI). MethodsSeventy-three participants with a clinical diagnosis of AD or MCI, neuromelanin-sensitive MRI, and subsequent neuropathologic assessment from the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative were studied. At autopsy, 33 participants had LB pathology (LB+) and 40 had no LB pathology (LB-). We compared SNc volume between groups using analysis of covariance adjusted for age and sex. Within the LB+ group, we assessed the association between SNc volume and nigral hypopigmentation using Spearman correlation. In a secondary analysis, we tested whether adding SNc volume to a logistic regression mode containing age, sex, and executive function improved model fit for autopsy-defined LB status. ResultsLB+ participants had greater nigral hypopigmentation at autopsy and lower antemortem SNc volume than LB- participants. The adjusted mean difference in SNc volume (LB+ minus LB-) was -66 mm3 (95% confidence interval -115.9 to -16.2, P=0.010). Within the LB+ group, lower SNc volume was associated with greater hypopigmentation (Spearman {rho}=-0.373, P=0.032). Among 71 participants with complete model data, adding SNc volume improved model fit (likelihood ratio {chi}2(1)=8.67, P=0.003). The combined model had an in sample area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.770 (95% confidence interval: 0.661-0.879). ConclusionThe correspondence between lower antemortem SNc volume and greater hypopigmentation at autopsy supports the use of neuromelanin-sensitive MRI to characterize nigral involvement in AD or MCI with LB copathology. These findings are based on a single cohort, and the interval of several years between imaging and autopsy limits how closely the pigmentation ratings reflect nigral integrity at imaging.

papers.title: Anatomical and Etiologic Predictors of Oculopalatal Tremor Phenotypes: A Pooled Patient-Level Analysis
papers.abstract: Oculopalatal tremor (OPT) follows disruption of the cerebello-rubro-olivary network and is frequently associated with hypertrophic inferior-olive degeneration (HOD). HOD does not invariably produce OPT; determinants of oculo-palatal, ocular-only, palatal-only, or non-oscillatory phenotypes remain undefined. We analyzed 501 patients with HOD, of which 424 with classifiable laterality: 52.1% had unilateral and 47.9% bilateral HOD. Lesion location predicted HOD laterality (chi-square=35.65, p=3.4x10^-7; Cramer V=0.31): brainstem/pons lesions produced ipsilateral HOD in 70.0%, whereas cerebellar lesions produced contralateral HOD in 86.4%. Bilateral HOD reflected combined cerebellar/brainstem lesions, and was associated with ocular oscillations (OR 2.66, 95% CI 1.31-5.43; p=0.0067) but not convincingly palatal oscillations (OR 1.49, 95% CI 0.91-2.42; p=0.137). Phenotype differed by etiology (p=0.0024): hemorrhagic and vascular-malformation lesions preferentially produced combined OPT, ischemic lesions were enriched among ocular-only presentations, and neoplastic lesions produced the most heterogeneous phenotype and were disproportionately represented among palatal-only cases. Age, sex, and lesion laterality were not associated with phenotype. Four-class prediction was limited (macro AUC 0.555; balanced accuracy 0.301), with little improvement after adding HOD laterality (macro AUC 0.563; balanced accuracy 0.323). Among classifiable OPT waveforms, 96.9% contained a pendular component. Median OPT latency was 6 months (IQR 4.75-24); lesion location, etiology, and HOD laterality did not predict latency. HOD is therefore an important substrate, but lesion anatomy and etiology shape group-level phenotype without enabling reliable individual prediction.

papers.title: Integrating Plasma Brain-Derived pTau217, White Matter Hyperintensity and Hippocampal Volumes as Optimized Prognostic Markers for Cognitive Decline in an Asian Cohort with High Cerebrovascular Disease Burden
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Combination of plasma and neuroimaging biomarkers associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and cerebrovascular pathophysiology might provide more accurate prediction of cognitive decline in populations with extensive AD and cerebral small vessel disease copathologies. Here, we aimed to identify an optimized biomarker panel for predicting cognitive decline by evaluating combinations of plasma and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) biomarkers. Methods: We investigated participants without dementia or with mild dementia, recruited from memory clinics and the community in Singapore between August 2010 and August 2020. Plasma biomarkers of brain amyloid (brain-derived [BD]-pTau217, BD-pTau181, BD-pTau231, total-pTau217, total-pTau181, and total-pTau231), astrogliosis (GFAP), and neuroaxonal injury (NfL), with MRI measures of cerebrovascular disease (white matter hyperintensity [WMH] volume) and neurodegeneration (hippocampal volume), and primary outcome of longitudinal Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB; mean [SD] follow-up duration, 51.0 [15.8] months). All plasma and MRI biomarker combinations for predicting CDR-SB slope (annual change in CDR-SB) were evaluated. Results: This study included 523 participants (mean [SD] age, 72.4 [7.9] years; 291 females [55.6%]). The parsimonious model included plasma BD-pTau217, WMH volume, and hippocampal volume (all P [≤] 0.004). Dichotomizing these biomarkers yielded A, V, and N status, respectively, classifying participants as all negative (A-V-N-; n = 128), 1-positive (A+V-N-, A-V+N- or A-V-N+; n = 154), 2-positive (A+V+N-, A+V-N+, A-V+N+;n = 158) or 3-positive (A+V+N+; n = 83). Annual CDR-SB progression increased stepwise with the number of positive biomarkers. Compared with the all negative group ({beta}, 0.016), the 1-positive ({beta}, 0.409), 2-positive ({beta}, 1.16) and 3-positive groups ({beta}, 1.49) showed faster cognitive decline (all P < 0.001). Moreover, the 2-positive and 3-positive groups progressed faster than the 1-positive group (both P < 0.001), and the 3-positive group declined faster than 2-positive group (P = 0.009). Conclusions: Presence of multiple pathophysiological processes was associated with greater cognitive decline, highlighting the utility of a comprehensive multimodal biomarker profile to enhance prognostication.

papers.title: APOE ϵ4 Effects on Cognitive Decline and Progression to Dementia are Sequentially Mediated through Plasma P-tau217 and Hippocampal Atrophy in an Asian Cohort
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe APOE {varepsilon}4 allele is a major genetic risk factor for Alzheimers disease (AD) but underlying pathophysiological mechanisms may vary across populations. In Asian cohorts, the relative contributions of plasma phosphorylated tau (p-tau217), neurodegeneration, and cerebrovascular disease to {varepsilon}4-associated cognitive decline remain unclear. ObjectiveWe investigated biomarker pathways linking APOE {varepsilon}4 to cognitive trajectories and incident dementia. MethodsAPOE genotyping, plasma p-tau217 measurement, and neuroimaging were conducted at baseline in the Singapore Harmonization longitudinal cohort. Participants underwent annual comprehensive neuropsychological assessments for five years. We examined {varepsilon}4 group differences in p-tau217, regional subcortical volumes, cortical thickness, and white matter hyperintensities (WMH). Serial mediation analyses examined mediating effects of plasma p-tau217 and neuroimaging markers on {varepsilon}4 associations with cognitive decline and dementia risk. ResultsAPOE {varepsilon}4 was present in 29.4% of cohort (N=659; age=73.5{+/-}8.0 years; female=56.4%; Chinese ethnicity=83.6%). Carriers had higher p-tau217, reduced entorhinal thickness, and smaller hippocampus, amygdala, accumbens, and putamen volumes, but no WMHdifferences. Pathways from APOE {varepsilon}4 through p-tau217 to hippocampal volume ({beta}=- 0.009, 95% CI=-0.015, -0.004, 13.8%) and entorhinal thickness ({beta}=-0.008, 95% CI=- 0.014, -0.004, 13%) significantly mediated steeper global and domain-specific cognitive decline. APOE {varepsilon}4 was associated with increased dementia risk (HR=2.35, 95% CI=1.37-4.06), partially mediated by p-tau217 and hippocampal volume (9%). Direct {varepsilon}4 effects were minimal and WMH did not influence these associations. ConclusionsAPOE {varepsilon}4 contributes to cognitive decline and incident dementia through an AD-specific cascade captured by increased p-tau217 and hippocampal atrophy, providing population-specific insights into APOE {varepsilon}4-related pathways in older Asian adults.

papers.title: Automated Classification of Clinical EEG Reports as Normal or Pathological Using Natural Language Processing: A Multi-Centre Study
papers.abstract: AO_SCPLOWBSTRACTC_SCPLOWWe evaluated automated classification of 6,829 de-identified free-text EEG reports from 33 Polish hospitals, independently rated by three experts. Three NLP models--fine-tuned PolBERT, a TF-IDF support vector classifier (SVC), and CatBoost--were assessed across seven binary and three-class tasks. Reference labels were derived from mean expert scores, majority voting or the Dawid-Skene (D-S) model, with different treatments of uncertain cases. Inter-rater agreement was moderate (Krippendorffs = 0.585) and below intra-rater agreement (Cohens {kappa} = 0.731-0.769); D-S skill rankings differed from unweighted intra-rater {kappa} rankings. PolBERT led on six of seven tasks (binary accuracy 0.876-0.952), although its advantage over CatBoost on three-class tasks was not significant. On Task 2A, all models exceeded all individual experts (0.762- 0.774 vs 0.689-0.726). Binary accuracy held at two isolated hospitals; on Task 2A, SVC fell from 0.762 to 0.616, while PolBERT reached 0.797. Errors clustered in disputed reports (accuracy 0.663-0.771 in intermediate strata). Exploratory zero-shot Qwen3.8-27B achieved binary accuracy of 0.829-0.929, below supervised models, and agreed with experts similarly to their mutual agreement ({kappa} = 0.53-0.61 vs 0.47-0.63), but favoured pathological labels. Automated classification of Polish clinical EEG reports is feasible across centres, with performance comparable to individual experts. Model probabilities were well calibrated (ECE [≤] 0.035), supporting threshold-based triage. Accuracy depends on expert disagreement and the method used to construct reference labels; label aggregation should therefore be part of the task definition.

papers.title: Chronic pain and cognitive performance in dementia caregivers: Insights from the STELLA and DETECT-AD studies
papers.abstract: BACKGROUNDApproximately 75% of individuals with Alzheimers disease and related dementias rely on informal caregivers, yet caregiver health, including chronic pain, remains under-addressed. Chronic pain is highly prevalent, functionally limiting, and linked to cognitive vulnerability, but remains understudied in informal caregivers. This study examined differences in pain and cognitive performance between caregivers and non-caregivers. OBJECTIVETo compare chronic pain and cognitive performance between dementia caregivers and non-caregivers and determine whether differences persist independent of age. METHODSWe conducted a secondary analysis of longitudinal data from STELLA and DETECT-AD. Ninety-five participants were followed for 12 months. Weekly online questionnaires assessed pain intensity (0-10 scale) and pain interference (Likert scale), while annual in-person evaluations measured cognition using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Group differences were evaluated using t-tests and multivariate regression adjusting for age. RESULTSGroups were similar in sex and education but differed in age, pain, and cognition. Caregivers were significantly younger (71.3 vs 77.3 years; p < 0.0001) and caregivers demonstrated significantly higher global cognitive performance as measured by the MoCA (mean score 26.8 vs 25.2; p = 0.02). After age adjustment, caregivers reported significantly higher pain intensity (OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.00-2.01; p = 0.048). CONCLUSIONSDementia caregivers exhibit greater pain burden despite younger age, highlighting chronic pain as a critical, underrecognized dimension of caregiver health and identifying an important opportunity to expand existing telehealth caregiver support models. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRY NAME, URL, AND REGISTRATION NUMBERSTELLA: ClinicalTrials.gov, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05338710, NCT04335110 DETECT: ClinicalTrials.gov, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05385913

papers.title: Hypothesis-Driven Thalamic Stereo-EEG Informs Surgical Therapy for Drug-Resistant Epilepsy: Outcomes in 117 Consecutive Patients
papers.abstract: ObjectiveThalamic stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG) is used to characterize seizure networks and guide neuromodulation, yet its safety and clinical utility are incompletely characterized. We examined how thalamic SEEG informs surgical therapy. MethodsWe reviewed 117 consecutive patients who underwent thalamic SEEG at Massachusetts General Hospital (2020-2025), in whom the anterior (ANT), centromedian (CM), or pulvinar (PUL) nucleus was sampled to test a seizure network hypothesis. We assessed complications, targeting accuracy, the effect of thalamic ictal timing on laterality determination and neuromodulation target selection, and seizure outcomes. ResultsSmall hemorrhages were seen on postoperative imaging for 0.3% of leads (4/1507); all were asymptomatic and none involved a thalamic lead. Targeting accuracy for ANT, CM, and PUL was 81.0%, 94.2%, and 100%, respectively. Early bilateral thalamic ictal signals identified bilateral seizure networks with 75.6% sensitivity and 78.1% specificity, rising to 92.6% sensitivity when bitemporal onset was excluded. Among 52 patients planned for thalamic or thalamocortical responsive neurostimulation (RNS), the pre-SEEG target was revised in 34.6%, including in patients whose cortical hypothesis was unchanged. Most cortical seizure-onset zones did not map to a single thalamic nucleus. Among patients treated with thalamic or thalamocortical RNS, those with early thalamic ictal signals had better seizure outcomes than those without (standardized mean difference 1.71, 95% CI 0.77-2.65). Mean primary seizure reduction was 75.0 {+/-} 31.7% after RNS (seizure freedom 40.4%) and 90.9 {+/-} 20.6% after resection or laser interstitial thermal therapy (61.8%). SignificanceThalamic SEEG has a safety profile similar to that of non-thalamic SEEG, provides patient-specific information that informs neuromodulation strategy and target selection, and identifies an early thalamic ictal signal that is associated with better seizure outcomes. These findings support hypothesis-driven thalamic sampling in the evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy. KEY POINTSO_LINo hemorrhage occurred with 373 thalamic SEEG leads, and ANT, CM, and PUL were targeted accurately. C_LIO_LIEarly bilateral thalamic ictal signals identify bilateral seizure networks (75.6% sensitivity, 78.1% specificity). C_LIO_LIThe thalamic RNS target changed in 34.6% of RNS candidates, including in patients whose cortical hypothesis was unchanged. C_LIO_LICortical seizure-onset zones do not map exclusively to a single thalamic nucleus. C_LIO_LIAn early thalamic ictal signal on SEEG is associated with better outcomes after thalamic RNS. C_LI

papers.title: At-home ankle and wrist accelerometry and machine learning capture motor impairment and disease progression in ataxia-telangiectasia
papers.abstract: BackgroundAtaxia-telangiectasia (A-T) is a rare, childhood-onset neurodegenerative disorder for which sensitive, age-appropriate motor outcome measures are needed to support emerging clinical trials. Clinician-rated ataxia scales are limited by subjectivity, low granularity, and floor and ceiling effects. We evaluated whether at-home wearable accelerometry, combined with machine-learned composite scores derived from submovement features, captures cross-sectional motor impairment and longitudinal disease progression in A-T. Methods43 children with classic A-T (median age 9.0 years; IQR 5.7-13.4) and 50 age- and sex-matched controls wore GENEActiv accelerometers on the ankle and wrist during one week of natural behavior at home, repeated at 6- to 12-month intervals. From 85 submovement, activity-intensity, and spectral features per sensor site, we trained composite severity models targeting the Brief Ataxia Rating Scale (BARS) gait subscore (ankle) and BARS total score (wrist). FindingsAnkle composite scores correlated strongly with BARS gait (r = 0.88), BARS total (r = 0.88), and caregiver-reported CPCHILD (r = -0.69); wrist composite scores correlated with BARS total (r = 0.88), BARS arm (r = 0.84), and CPCHILD (r = -0.78). Both models discriminated A-T from controls with large effect sizes (ankle Cohens d = 2.28; wrist d = 2.98) and demonstrated excellent within-week reliability (ICC = 0.95 ankle; 0.92 wrist). The ankle composite captured disease progression sensitively (Mean-to-Standard Deviation Ratio [MSDR] = 0.98; p < 0.0001). In a matched subset with both sensor and clinical data, ankle composite slopes significantly captured progression (Wilcoxon vs zero, p = 0.0036), whereas BARS total (p = 0.079) and BARS gait (p = 0.30) did not. InterpretationAt-home ankle-based wearable accelerometry provides a sensitive, interpretable, and ecologically valid measure of motor function and disease progression in A-T and may serve as a candidate outcome measure for clinical trials. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed and Google Scholar for articles published up to September 2026 using the terms "ataxia-telangiectasia", "wearable", "accelerometer", "digital biomarker", and "motor outcome measure". Clinician-rated ataxia scales remain the standard for assessing motor severity in A-T, but are limited by rater subjectivity, low granularity, and age-dependent baseline scores in children. Task-based wearable assessments have shown promise but share the limitations of requiring structured protocols and participant cooperation. At-home wearable accelerometry using submovement analysis had been applied to the wrist in children with A-T in one prior study by our group, demonstrating cross-sectional validity and longitudinal change over one year. Ankle-worn sensors had been used to estimate ataxia severity in children with A-T during a supervised gait assessment, and at-home ankle-based submovement measures and machine-learned composite scores had shown strong sensitivity in adult cerebellar ataxias. However, at-home composite scores and ankle-based measures had not been evaluated in A-T, and no study had compared ankle and wrist sensor sites in a pediatric A-T cohort or assessed longitudinal sensitivity of ankle-derived measures against clinician-rated scales in A-T. Added value of this studyIn an expanded pediatric cohort of 43 children with A-T and 50 controls followed for up to 5.8 years, we show that machine-learned composite scores derived from ankle and wrist accelerometer data collected during natural behavior at home correlate strongly with clinician-rated ataxia severity and caregiver-reported function, distinguish A-T from controls across age groups, and demonstrate high within-week reliability. The ankle composite captured disease progression with higher sensitivity than clinician-rated BARS, including in non-ambulatory individuals, whereas the wrist composite did not reach significance as a longitudinal measure. Both models identified a consistent motor signature of ataxia across upper and lower limbs. Implications of all the available evidencePassive at-home ankle accelerometry combined with submovement-based machine learning provides a sensitive, low-burden, and scalable measure of motor function and disease progression in A-T. This approach could complement clinician-rated scales as an objective outcome measure to increase clinical trial efficiency and provide early evidence for treatment efficacy. The low-cost single-sensor design supports geographically distributed trial enrollment, which is particularly relevant for rare diseases like A-T.

papers.title: Focal surgical lesions reveal a subthalamic substrate for human wakefulness
papers.abstract: How focal subthalamic injury disrupts a distributed arousal system remains incompletely understood. We investigated transient somnolence after unilateral pallidothalamic tractotomy without sedation in 56 patients, including 14 with somnolence. Volume-adjusted probabilistic lesion mapping identified a hotspot dorsal to the lateral hypothalamus (MNI -6.0, -10.5, -4.0 mm; family-wise error-corrected P = 0.011). A model combining peak involvement and log-transformed lesion volume achieved a leave-one-out cross-validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.799. Applied without refitting to two external cohorts comprising 19 patients, it achieved an AUC of 0.830 (95% confidence interval 0.636-0.977; two-sided cohort-stratified exact permutation P = 0.0166). In a supplementary analysis, somnolence-associated lesions had greater map-weighted burden within a published structural connectivity map of consciousness recovery after deep brain stimulation (P = 0.0299). These findings identify a focal subthalamic vulnerability in maintaining human wakefulness, with a lesion-based model discriminating transient somnolence in independent surgical patients.

papers.title: Plasma proteomic markers of cognitive and brain aging in a multi-ethnic cohort
papers.abstract: Advances in ultrasensitive proteomics offer opportunities to characterize molecular pathways underlying brain aging. We measured 220 plasma proteins using NULISAseq Neuro220 in 250 Chinese, South Asian, and non-Hispanic White older adults (mean age=68.2 years; 70.4% female). Proteins implicated in neurodegenerative diseases (including brain-derived phosphorylated Tau; BDpTau), synaptic function, oxidative stress, and inflammation were associated with poorer cognition. Phosphorylated Tau205 was associated with reduced entorhinal thickness, whereas inflammatory proteins were associated with imaging markers of cerebral small vessel disease. Several findings were replicated in 1,381 participants in the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, including associations of BDpTau species, NPTX2, BACE1, TREM1, CCL17, PRDX6, and IGF1R with cognitive decline and clinical progression. Cardiometabolic risk factors were associated with widespread proteomic alterations, many of which were also linked to poorer brain health. These results identify promising molecular markers of brain aging and extend proteomic research to ethnically diverse populations historically underrepresented in Alzheimers disease research.

papers.title: Disease-specific versus symptom-specific neuroimaging phenotypes across Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, and Small Vessel Disease
papers.abstract: BackgroundNeurodegenerative disorders are common in ageing populations, and arise from several distinct pathophysiological causes. Yet, they also share many symptoms, including cognitive and neuropsychiatric ones. It is unclear to what extent the impact of neurodegeneration on brain systems is unique or shared across disorders, and whether shared symptoms are driven by degeneration of the same brain systems. MethodsWe collected data from n=251 participants with Alzheimers Disease, Parkinsons Disease, Small Vessel Disease, and age-matched healthy controls. All participants underwent harmonized cognitive and neuropsychiatric assessment and were scanned using the UK-Biobank MRI protocol capturing features including brain volume, white matter lesions and microstructure, tract volume, iron content, and functional connectivity. ResultsWe replicated established case-control brain changes in Alzheimers Disease, Parkinsons Disease and Small Vessel Disease compared to healthy controls. Leveraging this joint standardised dataset, we identified distinct neuroimaging features of individual neurodegenerative disorders, providing evidence for robust diagnosis-specific brain changes. Importantly, however, there was also a large degree of transdiagnostic similarity across neuroimaging markers. Testing for transdiagnostic associations between symptoms and brain phenotypes, we found that lower medial frontal pole connectivity to primary motor cortex was preferentially associated with apathy, fatigue, and depression; whereas cingulum microstructure was associated with cognitive deficits across diagnoses. ConclusionsThese results demonstrate that different neurodegenerative diseases are characterised by dissociable brain changes, but also common transdiagnostic and symptom-associated features. This suggests that shared symptoms across neurodegeneration may in part be driven by overlapping impact on key brain systems, such as changes in medial frontal pole connectivity and cingulum microstructure. Our work highlights that multimodal imaging biomarkers can help understand and parse symptomatic heterogeneity in neurodegenerative and ageing populations.

papers.title: Generalizable mapping of the Epileptogenic Zone from interictal Intracranial EEG using an implant topology-aware Transformer
papers.abstract: Presurgical localization of the epileptogenic zone remains a central challenge in drug-resistant focal epilepsy. At the same time, the abundant interictal intracranial EEG (iEEG) data routinely acquired during presurgical evaluation remain an underexploited source of localizing information. We developed an iEEG implant topology-aware transformer that combines interictal iEEG features with electrode coordinates to predict resection targets. The model was trained exclusively on three public datasets (n = 476) and tested on cohorts from five independent centers across three countries (n = 216). In patients with favorable surgical outcomes (Engel I; n = 120), the median area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) was 0.71, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.92, outperforming interictal spike rate and clinically defined seizure-onset zone baselines in patients with favorable outcomes (P < 0.05 for both AUPRC and AUROC). Patients with unfavorable outcomes (Engel II-IV; n = 96) had lower prediction-resection alignment (median AUPRC, 0.42), and their highest-confidence predictions were located farther from resected tissue (P = 0.005). These findings establish a generalizable framework that integrates neural activity and brain topology to identify epileptogenic tissue from interictal recordings, potentially improving surgical success rates and reducing reliance on resource-intensive seizure capture.
